extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards for evaluating whether a patent application's specification meets the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA first paragraph). Focuses on how examiners should analyze claims, the specification, embodiments, drawings, and other disclosures to determine whether applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as of the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental factual inquiry: possession as of filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental factual inquiry is whether the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess possession from standpoint of one of ordinary skill as of filing date. Cases: Vas-Cath, AbbVie v. Janssen, In re Smith, In re Wertheim. The inquiry is factual and case-by-case; how close the description must come depends on the nature of the invention and the knowledge imparted to those skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption and examiner's initial burden / making a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description is present in the specification as filed; the examiner has the initial burden, after thorough reading/evaluation, of presenting evidence or reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize adequate support for the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make a prima facie case the examiner must identify claim limitations that are not adequately supported and explain why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure. A clear, specific explanation (e.g., that the specification lists each element but lacks adequate description of their combination) can shift burden to applicant. See Wertheim; Hyatt v. Dudas; Stored Value Solutions v. Card Activation Techs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction and analyze claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers; claim construction is essential and each claim must be separately analyzed and given a reasonable interpretation consistent with the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider entire claim including preamble, transitional phrase (comprising / consisting essentially of / consisting of), and body. Determine weight to be given the preamble and do not import limitations from the specification into the claims. Guidance and examples: In re Katz; Lockwood; Bell Communications; Corning Glass Works; Genentech v. Chiron; PPG Indus. v. Guardian Indus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review entire application to find support for claimed elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the claims and the entire specification (including specific embodiments, figures, sequence listings) to understand how applicant provides support for each element or step of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how disclosure supports various features; determine field of invention and level of skill. Information well known in the art need not be disclosed in detail. Compare embodiments, figures, and sequence listings to claims. See Rasmussen, Amgen v. Chugai, Wang Labs v. Toshiba.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession shown by actual reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention (constructed embodiment or performed process that meets all claim limitations and demonstrates the invention works for its intended purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to practice provides strong evidence of possession. Cases: Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder v. L’Oreal; Mahurkar. For biological materials, a deposit (37 CFR 1.801 et seq.) can evidence reduction to practice. Examiner should determine whether specification shows actual reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession shown by drawings or structural chemical formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by a clear depiction of the invention in detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas that permit a person skilled in the art to recognize applicant had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings alone may satisfy the written description requirement where they flesh out words. See Vas-Cath; In re Wolfensperger; Autogiro; Eli Lilly re generic formulae for chemical genus. Evaluate sufficiency of drawings and formulas for enabling identification of the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession shown by relevant identifying characteristics (biotech/chem specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate written description may be shown by description of sufficient, relevant, identifying characteristics (sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, etc.) that would permit a skilled artisan to recognize applicant was in possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In biotech, structural formulas are convenient but other combinations of identifying characteristics may suffice; examples include unique cleavage, isoelectric points, restriction maps, enzymatic activity comparisons, antibody cross-reactivity. However, function-only descriptions typically will not suffice for compositions (Eli Lilly, Fiers). See Enzo Biochem; Falkner v. Inglis; Capon v. Eshhar; Amgen v. Sanofi; Centocor v. Abbott.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function plus a well-established structure–function correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement may be satisfied through disclosure of function and minimal structure when there is a well-established correlation between structure and function such that one skilled in the art can predict structure from recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the art has a strong structure-function correlation, functional recitation plus minimal structural detail may show possession (Enzo Biochem; Written Description Guidelines). Without such correlation, function-only disclosure is insufficient and is merely a wish or plan. See Eli Lilly; In re Wilder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-(or step-)plus-function limitations: corresponding structure/materials/acts required
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph), it must be interpreted to cover corresponding structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification and equivalents thereof; the specification must link particular structure/material/acts to the claimed function or it must be clear to one skilled in the art what disclosed structure performs the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings for corresponding structure. Two ways to satisfy: (1) written description adequately links/associates particular structure/material/acts to perform the function; or (2) it is clear that one skilled in the art would know which structures perform the recited function. If no corresponding structure is disclosed and the claim is indefinite under 112(b), it also fails 112(a) written description. Cases: Aristocrat Techs.; Atmel; Biomedino; In re Noll. See also MPEP §2181 and Fed. Reg. guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of conventional or well-known subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: What is conventional or well known to one of ordinary skill in the art need not be disclosed in detail; the written description requirement is applied in the context of the particular invention and the state of knowledge in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance between what is known and what is added evolves with the field. In mature technologies with high skill, less specificity in the specification may be required. See Hybritech; Capon v. Eshhar; Vas-Cath; Martin v. Johnson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species claims: three-step analysis (A,B,C) for single embodiment/species
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment or species, determine (A) whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, whether the invention is complete as evidenced by reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed to show possession; (C) if not, whether distinguishing identifying characteristics are disclosed in sufficient detail to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If complete structure is disclosed, written description is satisfied for that species. If not, evaluate whether other identifying characteristics (partial structure, properties, function+correlation, method of making) are detailed enough for a skilled artisan to recognize possession. If none of (A)-(C) are met, reject claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). See Fields v. Conover; Eli Lilly; In re Wilder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims: representative species or identifying characteristics required
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims drawn to a genus, the written description may be satisfied by sufficient description of a representative number of species (by reduction to practice or drawings) or by disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with known correlation) sufficient to show applicant was in possession of the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether representative species or species-characterizing features are disclosed so that a person skilled in the art would understand the scope of the genus. See Eli Lilly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in assessing possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider multiple factors: level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or with structure–function correlation, method of making, and combinations of such characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors to determine whether disclosed characteristics distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead a skilled artisan to conclude applicant had possession. Consider maturity of the art and reliance on patents/printed publications to determine what is known. In unpredictable arts more evidence is required. See Eli Lilly; Capon v. Eshhar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process and unpredictable fields: additional evidence required
rubrics_metrics.description: For product-by-process claims and inventions in unpredictable arts (e.g., certain biological and chemical inventions), disclosure of only a method of making and function may not suffice; where the process has been used to produce the product, written description is satisfied, but if it is unclear that acts can be performed or product produced, the requirement may not be met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unpredictable fields, disclosure of additional characterization may still be insufficient if inventor cannot define or obtain the product; reduction to practice may be the only convincing evidence. See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen v. Chugai; Burroughs Wellcome v. Barr Labs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly added or amended claims: applicant must point out original support
rubrics_metrics.description: For newly added or amended claims applicant should show support in the original disclosure for the new or amended claims; an examiner can state that applicant has not pointed out where support exists when support is not apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple statement that applicant has not pointed out where the new/amended claim is supported may be sufficient where support is not apparent; applicant should specifically point out support for any amendments. See Hyatt v. Dudas; MPEP §§ 714.02, 2163.04, 2163.06.
